studies.title: Showing shoppers the math: making hidden tier discounts visible lifted subscriptions on a health platform
studies.paper_title: Discount display in tiered pricing: Nudging subscriptions in online healthcare services
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Researchers exploited a quasi-natural experiment on a major Chinese online healthcare platform that redesigned its subscription interface so the savings implied by longer, higher-tier plans were displayed explicitly rather than left for patients to calculate. Using an intensity-based difference-in-differences design across physicians' listings, they found that making the discount salient significantly increased patient subscriptions. The effect was not explained by physicians cutting prices or by other simultaneous platform changes, and it was concentrated among doctors treating a high share of chronic conditions, disappearing for mostly episodic care.
studies.why_it_matters: The prices did not change — only the display did — yet demand moved, suggesting that a large share of the value in tiered pricing is lost simply because customers will not do the cross-tier arithmetic themselves.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you sell in tiers — subscriptions, bundles, multi-packs, annual-versus-monthly — test spelling out the implied saving on each tier instead of leaving it implicit. This is a single-platform observational result, not a guaranteed lift, so treat it as a cheap A/B test worth running rather than a settled rule, and note that it worked for recurring, predictable needs and not for one-off purchases.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A reminder for shoppers: when a seller shows you how much you 'save' by committing longer, the underlying prices have not changed at all. The only thing that moved was how easy the comparison was to make — and that was enough to change what people bought.
studies.caveats: Single platform in a single country (China) and a single category (online healthcare); quasi-experimental rather than randomized, so unobserved concurrent changes cannot be fully ruled out despite the authors' checks.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, mechanism checks, moderator and caveats all match the abstract; causal language is appropriately hedged as quasi-experimental.

studies.title: Grocery subscriptions: shoppers want the mental break more than the time savings
studies.paper_title: Why (not) subscribe? Drivers and barriers of grocery replenishment subscriptions
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Using quota-representative consumer surveys in Germany (N=493) and the UK (N=339), researchers tested a value-versus-risk framework for automatic grocery replenishment subscriptions, pitting four benefits (time efficiency, supply reliability, cognitive relief, cost efficiency) against four matching worries (time concerns, supply mismatch, lock-in, financial concerns). Benefits explained considerably more variance in perceived usefulness and attitude than the barriers did, but financial concerns and fear of getting the wrong quantities still had strong negative effects. Notably, 'cognitive relief' — not having to remember or decide — outweighed pure time savings as a driver of perceived usefulness.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers pushing replenishment subscriptions typically market generic 'convenience,' but the data suggest convenience is multidimensional and the most persuasive component is the removal of mental load, not minutes saved.
studies.story_angle_primary: Rewrite subscription messaging around specific, concrete relief — 'never think about coffee again' — rather than vague convenience claims, and pair it with explicit risk defusers (easy skipping, flexible quantities, visible cancellation) because benefit messaging alone leaves the two biggest objections, cost and wrong-quantity deliveries, untouched. Test messaging by market maturity: the German and UK patterns were similar but not identical.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Consumers report being genuinely ambivalent about auto-replenishment: they like it and distrust it at the same time. The sticking points are not whether it saves time but whether you will be locked in and whether you will end up with six bottles of detergent you did not need.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey measuring stated usage intention, not actual subscription behavior or spending; cannot establish causation; limited to two Western European markets.
studies.verdict_notes: Samples, drivers/barriers and the cognitive-relief finding are reported correctly; only the modelling description is loose.

studies.title: The psychology of the subscription you never use but can't cancel
studies.paper_title: Why we stay subscribed: interdependent self-construal as a driver of subscription retention in the digital economy
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.the_study: Across five studies — one correlational survey plus four experiments manipulating self-construal — researchers examined who keeps paying for subscriptions they no longer use. People primed toward an interdependent self-construal (defining themselves through relationships) were significantly more likely to retain an unused subscription involving other people than those primed toward an independent self-construal. Crucially, the effect was specific to retention: self-construal did not affect willingness to acquire a new subscription or to make a one-time purchase of a comparable social product.
studies.why_it_matters: Churn may be driven less by perceived value than by whether cancelling feels like severing a social bond, which points retention efforts toward relational framing rather than discounts.
studies.story_angle_primary: Churn-reduction teams could test whether surfacing the social dimension of a service — shared accounts, family plans, friends also using it, group activity — reduces cancellations more cheaply than win-back discounts. These are lab-style manipulations, so the honest next step is a live retention test, not a rollout, and the same logic says relational framing will do little to win new subscribers.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you are paying for something you never open, the reason may not be laziness or forgetting — it may be that cancelling feels like dropping a connection to other people. Worth asking yourself whether you are buying a service or buying out of a relationship.
studies.caveats: Experimental manipulations of self-construal with likely online-panel participants and hypothetical retention decisions rather than observed cancellations; sample sizes and nationality not specified in the abstract; stated choices rather than real money.
studies.verdict_notes: Five studies (one survey, four experiments), the retention-specific effect and the acquisition/one-time-purchase boundary conditions are all faithfully reported; caveats correctly flag unreported sample details.

studies.title: When every product looks the same, promotion and CRM are what investors pay for
studies.paper_title: Marketing strategy and firm value under commoditization
studies.the_study: Researchers built and validated text-based measures of how heavily firms emphasize each of the four Ps plus customer relationship management in their corporate disclosures, then linked that emphasis to firm value while tracking how similar each firm's products were to rivals'. In highly commoditized product spaces, greater emphasis on the "intangible" differentiators — promotion and CRM — was associated with significantly higher firm value, while emphasis on product, price and place features showed no such effect. The advantage disappeared for firms under heavy financial distress, where investors appear to discount the future payoff of relationship and communication investments.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives a market-valuation argument for protecting brand and CRM budgets exactly when categories become hard to differentiate on specs or price — the moment finance teams are most tempted to cut them.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your category is commoditizing, test whether your differentiation story still leans on product and price claims that rivals can copy within a quarter, and look at how the market has rewarded peers who shifted emphasis toward promotion and customer relationships. The distress boundary condition is a warning: the same spending reads differently to investors when the balance sheet is shaky.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A quiet explanation for why so many near-identical products — insurance, coffee, consumer electronics — compete through advertising, apps and membership perks rather than through the product itself. Once the goods converge, the relationship is the product.
studies.caveats: Observational analysis of firm disclosures and valuations, so associations rather than proven causation; text-based measures of strategy emphasis capture what firms say they prioritize, which may diverge from actual spending; sample scope and period are not specified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Accurate on the core asymmetry and the distress boundary condition, but 'disappeared' overstates 'attenuated'.

studies.title: "Leave a 5-star review and get a discount" damages trust more than simply paying for honest feedback
studies.paper_title: The price of praise: How incentive conditionality drives perceived deception and erodes brand trust
studies.the_study: In a between-subjects experiment, participants saw a brand's review incentive message that either tied the reward to a favorable review (conditional) or offered the reward regardless of what the reviewer wrote (unconditional). Conditional incentives raised perceived deception and lowered brand trust, with perceived deception statistically mediating the effect. Counterintuitively, consumers with a higher general disposition to trust showed the sharpest rise in perceived deception when the reward was conditional.
studies.why_it_matters: The reputational cost of review incentive programs appears to hinge on a single line of copy — whether the payoff is conditional on praise — not on whether incentives exist at all.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit the wording of every review-solicitation email, insert card and post-purchase prompt for language that even implies a reward is contingent on positivity, and consider A/B testing conditional versus explicitly unconditional phrasing on trust and review volume. The finding that the most trusting customers react worst suggests your best advocates may be the ones you alienate.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers increasingly read the incentive behind the review, not just the review. An offer of a gift card for "your honest feedback" lands very differently from one that rewards five stars — and consumers are quietly keeping score.
studies.caveats: Single experiment using hypothetical incentive messages rather than real purchases or real review-writing behavior; sample size, composition and country are not reported in the abstract; measures brand trust attitudes rather than observed buying; moderation of the direct effect was only marginally supported.
studies.verdict_notes: Study description, mediation and the disposition-to-trust moderation are accurate, and the marginal direct-effect moderation is flagged; one consumer-angle claim goes beyond the data.

studies.title: Consistent prices across channels build lock-in; consistent promotions do nothing
studies.paper_title: How Channel Consistency Relates to Synergy Realisation and Within‐Firm Lock‐In in Omnichannel Grocery Retailing? A Mixed‐Methods Approach
studies.the_study: A mixed-methods study of Chinese omnichannel grocery shoppers tested five dimensions of cross-channel consistency — product, service, price, promotion and communication — against perceived synergy and "within-firm lock-in," using PLS-SEM in a quantitative phase followed by in-depth interviews. Product, service and price consistency were positively linked to both synergy and lock-in; communication consistency related only to synergy; promotion consistency related to neither. Regulatory focus (promotion versus prevention orientation) moderated only selected relationships.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers pouring effort into harmonizing offers across app, web and store may be optimizing the one dimension shoppers appear not to reward, while price parity does the heavier lifting on retention.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before the next omnichannel integration project, separate price parity from promotional parity and test them independently — this data suggests shoppers may tolerate (or even expect) channel-specific deals while punishing inconsistent base prices. Worth validating with your own transaction data before reallocating budget.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Most shoppers seem relaxed about app-only coupons and store-only specials, but notice when the shelf price and the online price don't match. The former reads as a deal; the latter reads as a trick.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey design, so causal direction cannot be established; single country (China) and single category (grocery); results are significant and non-significant paths in a structural model; sample size for the quantitative phase is not reported in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Path results and moderation are reported correctly, but the consumer angle reads a null path as positive shopper tolerance.

studies.title: Half of smokers don't flinch at price hikes — but plain packs reach them
studies.paper_title: Preferences on cigarette plain packaging among adults who smoke and adults who do not smoke: a discrete choice experiment in Chile
studies.the_study: Researchers ran an online discrete choice experiment with 1,029 Chilean adults (731 who smoke, 298 who do not), asking each to choose among cigarette packs varying in price, branded versus plain packaging, branded versus warning-labeled sticks, and licit versus illicit origin, with an opt-out. A latent class model found two very different groups of smokers: a price-sensitive 40% who actually preferred plain packs and warning sticks, and a 60% majority who were not significantly price-sensitive and preferred branded packs and sticks. Combining a 50% price increase with plain packaging and warning sticks cut predicted pack uptake among smokers by 7.7 percentage points, though illicit pack uptake rose 4.2 points.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows that a single lever — tax or packaging alone — reaches only part of a market, because consumers segment into distinct price-sensitive and brand-loyal groups that respond to opposite instruments.
studies.story_angle_primary: A reminder that price elasticity is rarely uniform across a customer base: this study suggests testing whether your own category splits into a discount-responsive segment and a design/brand-responsive one, and whether the two need entirely different levers. Also note the dark side — squeezing price pushed some demand toward illicit supply, a risk worth modeling in any aggressive pricing move.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Most smokers in this study said price wouldn't change their behavior, but packaging would — a sign of how much of what feels like a rational purchasing decision is actually driven by the look of the thing in your hand.
studies.caveats: Online panel with hypothetical choice sets rather than observed purchases; stated preferences only; single country (Chile); tobacco-specific and shaped by a live policy debate; smoker and non-smoker samples are unequal in size.
studies.verdict_notes: Latent-class percentages, the 7.7pp and 4.2pp figures and sample composition are correct; the headline rounds 60% down to 'half'.

studies.title: Explaining how the tracker works makes drivers more likely to accept it, not less
studies.paper_title: To share or not to share: an experimental study on telematics adoption in an insurance setting
studies.the_study: A randomized vignette experiment embedded in an online survey of 1,301 European motor insurance policyholders tested whether transparency about telematics data collection helps or hurts adoption. Half received a clear explanation of how telematics technology gathers and uses driving data before evaluating hypothetical policies; half did not. Transparency significantly raised purchase intentions, and while privacy concerns did create measurable disutility, premium discounts and value-added services largely offset it.
studies.why_it_matters: Firms often assume explaining data practices will spook customers; here disclosure acted as a modest driver of adoption, and discounts proved an effective currency for buying back privacy concerns.
studies.story_angle_primary: Insurers and any subscription business using behavioral data could A/B test upfront, plain-language explanations of data collection against vague terms-and-conditions framing — this evidence suggests clarity may be an acquisition asset rather than a liability. Quantify the discount needed to offset privacy disutility in your own category rather than guessing.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The experiment puts a price on privacy: people will trade driving data for a cheaper premium, and they're more willing when they actually understand the deal than when it's left unexplained.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical policies and stated purchase intentions, not actual take-up; online survey panel; European policyholders only; short time horizon with no measure of whether adoption persists after people live with being tracked.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample, design, direction of effect and the 'modest driver' framing all match; one unverifiable detail about group sizes.

studies.title: Nearly 4 in 10 cigarettes smoked in Bolivia's big cities are illicit — but taxes aren't the reason
studies.paper_title: Measuring illicit cigarette purchases in Bolivia: evidence from an intercept survey
studies.the_study: Researchers intercepted and surveyed 2,366 adult smokers in Bolivia's three largest metro areas (La Paz/El Alto, Cochabamba and Santa Cruz) in July–August 2024, photographing their actual cigarette packs and classifying them as illicit based on missing Bolivian tax registration numbers, non-compliant health warnings or absent customs stamps; loose-cigarette purchases were classified by brand authorization and price-outlier rules. An estimated 38.1% of consumption was illicit, with a single industrial-scale Paraguayan brand accounting for 85% of it. Penetration ranged from 54.4% in Santa Cruz to 10.4% in La Paz/El Alto — despite identical national tax rates — pointing to border proximity and enforcement gaps rather than price.
studies.why_it_matters: The tobacco industry's standard argument against tax increases is that they fuel smuggling; this is the first independent, pack-level estimate for Bolivia since 2002 and it undercuts that claim within a single tax jurisdiction.
studies.story_angle_primary: A case study in how to stress-test an industry talking point with observed product evidence rather than company-supplied sales data — and a reminder for any regulated category that distribution and enforcement, not price, can be the dominant driver of gray-market share.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you buy cigarettes in Santa Cruz, there's a better-than-even chance the pack never passed through legal channels — and the price you pay has little to do with your own country's tax policy.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey in a single country, limited to three metropolitan areas (not rural Bolivia); pack classification relies on visual markers and price rules; correlates of illicit purchase come from a probit model and are associational, not causal.
studies.verdict_notes: All headline numbers (38.1%, 85%, 54.4%, 10.4%), sample and method match; one phrasing about the 2002 benchmark is slightly off.

studies.title: Europe's supermarkets are selling nearly identical plant-based lineups — and pricing them inconsistently
studies.paper_title: Retailers as gatekeepers of the protein transition: commercialization patterns for plant-based meat alternatives in Europe
studies.the_study: Researchers audited the online stores of 17 retailers across five European countries, collecting 748 plant-based meat analogue products and coding format, ingredients, nutrition, price, on-pack claims, cooking instructions and visual elements, then applying factor and cluster analysis. Assortments turned out to be highly standardized across countries, with commercialization clustering into three pitches: sustainability credentials, dietary-lifestyle alignment, and a health-plus-taste combination. The authors flag thin brand variety, almost no fish analogues, limited recipe and flavor diversity, and inconsistent pricing and category labeling across retailers.
studies.why_it_matters: Retailers, not manufacturers, are the real gatekeepers of whether the plant-based category grows — and the audit suggests the category is being merchandised as a uniform block rather than managed with the pricing discipline and segmentation applied to established categories.
studies.story_angle_primary: For category managers: the findings imply white space in underrepresented segments (fish analogues, non-Western flavor profiles) and a pricing/classification problem worth auditing in your own shelf and e-commerce data — is the category priced coherently, or ad hoc?
studies.story_angle_secondary: Shoppers hunting for plant-based options will find much the same narrow selection whether they're in one European country or another, and the price logic between near-identical products often doesn't hold up.
studies.caveats: Descriptive audit of online assortments only — no sales, no consumer response, no causal test; five countries and 17 retailers may not represent the wider European market; online listings may differ from physical shelves; point-in-time snapshot.
studies.verdict_notes: Audit scope (748 products, 17 retailers, 5 countries) and the three commercialization clusters are accurate; one descriptor is stronger than the abstract.

studies.title: Making it cheaper isn't enough: how constant tradeoffs trap low-income shoppers
studies.paper_title: Consumption as disempowerment: enduring tradeoffs and eroding social capital in subsistence context
studies.the_study: In an interpretive qualitative study, researchers conducted in-depth interviews with subsistence consumers in a resource-constrained setting, analyzing how chronic scarcity shapes everyday purchase decisions. Three themes emerged — "making do with less," unstable intergenerational trajectories, and "listless existence" — which the authors theorize as "consumption entrapment": a self-reinforcing cycle in which repeated inadequate purchases erode the reciprocity, trust and mutual support networks people depend on.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the standard bottom-of-the-pyramid assumption that lower price points automatically empower poor consumers, arguing that affordability-only strategies can hollow out the community ties that keep households afloat.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brands serving low-income markets: a prompt to measure whether value-tier strategies actually improve customer outcomes and retention, or merely sustain a cycle of downgrading — and to consider cooperative, credit or savings-linked models alongside price cuts.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A window into what repeated small sacrifices at the till do to people over time — not just thinner shopping baskets, but fraying relationships and deferred ambitions.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interviews in one specific context with no stated sample size; interpretive design cannot establish causation or quantify effects; findings are theory-building rather than generalizable.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, themes and practical implications match the abstract; minor conflation of the paper's two distinct concepts (consumption entrapment vs. collapsing social capital).

studies.title: AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do — and the gap wrecks price optimization
studies.paper_title: How price sensitive is AI? Benchmarking LLM-generated willingness to pay in pricing analytics
studies.the_study: Researchers benchmarked willingness-to-pay figures generated by large language models acting as synthetic survey respondents against real willingness to pay elicited from human participants using the incentive-compatible Becker-DeGroot-Marschak mechanism, across four consumer product studies. They compared not just averages but full distributions, price-response curves, profit-maximizing prices and profit forecasts. For two more hedonic products the synthetic respondents systematically overstated willingness to pay and implied overly rosy demand and profit; for two utilitarian products results swung from roughly accurate to substantial underestimation. In every study the synthetic and real distributions differed significantly, meaning a matching average price can still hide a badly wrong demand curve.
studies.why_it_matters: Synthetic respondents are being sold as a cheap replacement for consumer research, but this evidence suggests they can produce plausible-looking numbers that lead to the wrong price — and the error direction is not predictable from the product alone.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your team is piloting LLM panels for pricing research, treat them as a hypothesis generator for early concept screening, not as an input to a final price point; test whether your own category shows the same hedonic over-optimism by running a small incentive-compatible validation against the synthetic numbers before trusting any profit forecast.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A window into how companies are starting to guess what you'd pay without ever asking you — and why the machine's guess tends to be more generous than a real person with real money on the line.
studies.caveats: Four product categories only; the comparison benchmark is a lab-style elicitation mechanism rather than observed market purchases; results may shift as LLMs are updated or prompted differently.
studies.verdict_notes: Body text faithfully reports the mixed direction of error, but the headline asserts only over-statement, which holds for the two hedonic products and not the utilitarian ones.

studies.title: For luxury NFTs, logos get clicks but only visual craft earns a price premium
studies.paper_title: Extending luxury into the NFT marketplace: The role of category typicality, brand prominence, and visual quality
studies.the_study: A 2x2x2 mixed-design experiment with 448 U.S. Millennial consumers tested how three design signals on luxury NFT collectibles — how typical the item is for the brand's category, how prominent the branding is, and the visual quality of the asset — affect willingness to buy and willingness to pay a premium. All three features raised willingness to buy, but only visual quality significantly raised willingness to pay more. Brand prominence also moderated typicality: the preference for category-typical NFTs faded when branding was subtle.
studies.why_it_matters: Luxury houses extending into digital collectibles have been leaning on logo visibility and familiar category cues, but the pricing power in this experiment came from execution quality rather than branding loudness.
studies.story_angle_primary: Separate the two jobs a digital collectible has to do: brand cues and category familiarity may drive trial and interest, while production quality is what the data suggest supports a premium price. Worth testing in live drops whether your highest-priced tiers differentiate on craft rather than on bigger logos.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Even in a market as speculative as digital collectibles, people appear to pay for how good something looks, not how clearly it's branded — a familiar instinct migrating into a new kind of shopping.
studies.caveats: Online experiment with hypothetical purchase and stated willingness to pay rather than real transactions; single country (U.S.) and single generational cohort (Millennials); NFT category sentiment is volatile and findings may be time-bound.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, N and main effects are accurate; the headline implies observed clicking behavior and the three-way interaction with visual quality is dropped.

studies.title: Opting out of data sharing may cost you: a model says privacy-protecting shoppers can end up paying more
studies.paper_title: Impact of the Invisibles: Personalized Pricing on Platform with Privacy-Preserving Users
studies.the_study: Economists built a two-stage game-theoretic model of an e-commerce platform that both designs customer segments and competes on price with third-party sellers on its own marketplace, in a world where a growing share of users refuse to share personal data. They identify a strategy they call "fuzzy segmentation," in which the platform lumps anonymous users together with selectively chosen data-sharing consumers. The result is that segmentation softens rather than intensifies price competition, and anonymous consumers can face a price premium in equilibrium — as can data-sharing consumers who prefer third-party sellers and get swept into the mixed segments.
studies.why_it_matters: It reframes privacy regulation as a pricing question: tighter data rules may hand platforms a new segmentation lever that raises prices for the very consumers the rules were meant to protect.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone running a marketplace or selling through one, the competitive implication is that how a platform groups unidentifiable users is itself a pricing weapon — third-party sellers should watch whether their most loyal customers are being quietly bundled into segments that erode their price advantage.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Refusing cookies and withholding data feels like a win, but this analysis suggests anonymity itself can become a signal retailers price against. Comparison shopping across sellers, not just privacy settings, is what protects your wallet.
studies.caveats: This is a purely analytical/theoretical model with no empirical data, no real platform transactions and no consumer behavior tested; conclusions follow from the model's assumptions about demand and competition and remain to be validated in actual markets.
studies.verdict_notes: Model, mechanism and equilibrium results are reported accurately and the theoretical status is clearly caveated; the consumer-facing advice goes slightly beyond the model.

studies.title: When AI learns from users, the free tier can start eating the business
studies.paper_title: Unlocking Profits in Generative AI: The Impact of AI Adaptive Learning on Freemium Strategy
studies.the_study: Researchers built an analytical model of how generative AI firms should structure freemium offers, accounting for the fact that AI improves through adaptive learning during fine-tuning — meaning free users both cannibalize paid demand and supply the data that makes the product better. The counterintuitive result: highly effective adaptive learning can reduce profitability, because it makes the free version so capable that it siphons off premium subscribers. The model also finds firms may rationally skip a free tier even when serving it costs almost nothing, cutting premium prices instead to grow the paid base, and that launching a free version does not reliably increase consumer welfare because better AI lets firms raise premium prices.
studies.why_it_matters: Freemium is the default playbook in generative AI, and this analysis argues the usual logic — free users pay you in training data — can reverse once the learning loop works too well.
studies.story_angle_primary: Pressure-test the assumption that your free tier pays for itself in data: the model implies there's a capability gap you have to actively manage between free and paid, and that a price cut on premium may sometimes beat giving the product away. Worth modeling against your own cohort conversion and inference-cost data.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Explains why free AI tools keep getting better and paid plans keep getting more expensive at the same time — your usage is improving the product, but that improvement is not necessarily passed back to you in price.
studies.caveats: Purely theoretical model with no empirical data from actual AI firms, pricing or user behavior; conclusions depend on modeling assumptions about cannibalization, service costs and learning effectiveness.
studies.verdict_notes: Core model results are reported accurately; the marketer angle paraphrases the capability-gap finding loosely and in a direction the abstract does not state.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Display beats price level.** "Showing shoppers the math" (W7220990040) finds that making tier savings explicit lifted subscriptions with no price change, converging with last run's "'Best before March 3' beats 'expires in 2 days'" (W7204248241) and "Same price, bigger discount" (W7172409631), where wording and reference framing moved demand at identical economics. Three consecutive sets of evidence now point the same way: the arithmetic shoppers are willing to do is the real constraint on pricing design.
- **Retention levers that cost nothing.** "The psychology of the subscription you never use but can't cancel" (W7215055600) sits directly alongside "Let them start today" (W7170377972): both locate churn in psychological attachment — relational bonds, psychological ownership — rather than in perceived value or discount depth.
- **Stated willingness to pay keeps failing its audit.** "AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do" (W7214644774) extends the methodological warning embedded in the cash-versus-card mega-replication (W7203715795), where spending moved reliably and stated willingness to pay did not. Two different literatures are now saying pricing research built on asked-for numbers is fragile.
- **Marketing budgets are defended on the balance sheet, not the brief.** "When every product looks the same, promotion and CRM are what investors pay for" (W7215085152) pairs with "When the stock market overvalues a company, marketing budgets are safer" (W7212389830) — both in *Journal of Business Research*, both finding that financial position, not marketing performance, determines whether brand and relationship spending survives.

**Advances**
- The fairness-of-pricing thread opened by Steam regional pricing (W7203929361) advances into retail with "Consistent prices across channels build lock-in; consistent promotions do nothing" (W7221526089): shoppers appear to police base-price parity while treating channel-specific deals as legitimate.
- The segmentation-of-response thread (income-conditioned grocery cutbacks, W7204997399; socioeconomic position and defaults, W7160239758) sharpens into formal latent classes in "Half of smokers don't flinch at price hikes" (W7215078694), where 60% of a market is effectively price-insensitive and responds only to design.
- The privacy-as-data-layer thread started by voice-inferred uncertainty (W7210283217) becomes an explicit pricing question in "Explaining how the tracker works makes drivers more likely to accept it" (W7214964045) and "Opting out of data sharing may cost you" (W4410534098).
- "Making it cheaper isn't enough" (W7204257214) deepens the distributional finding in W7204997399: low prices do not simply relieve constrained households, and may entrench the cycle.

**Counterpoints**
- Last run's "signals that backfire" cluster — voluntary freelancer guarantees (W4375826978) and employee discounts (W7170087457) — meets a split verdict here. "Explaining how the tracker works" (W7214964045) shows voluntary disclosure working as an acquisition asset rather than a red flag, while "'Leave a 5-star review and get a discount' damages trust" (W7221330457) confirms backfire but isolates the dividing line: conditionality, not the incentive itself.
- "A premium price drowns out your positioning story" (W7203839485) argued price overwhelms messaging; "For luxury NFTs, logos get clicks but only visual craft earns a price premium" (W7213234135) runs the other direction, with execution quality rather than price doing the premium work.

**New themes**
- Generative AI as a pricing actor, with no precedent in the previous digest: synthetic respondents distorting price optimization (W7214644774) and freemium design for self-improving AI products (W7213561739).
- Illicit trade and enforcement as pricing variables, via two *Tobacco Control* studies (W7215078694, W7215090900) — tax policy's limits where distribution, not price, drives market share.
- Category-level merchandising audits as a pricing story: "Europe's supermarkets are selling nearly identical plant-based lineups" (W7219001667) finds assortment uniformity plus incoherent pricing, a lens absent last run.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch describe pricing decisions being handed to software and to data postures rather than to shoppers. Synthetic AI respondents systematically misstate willingness to pay and corrupt profit forecasts ("AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do," W7214644774); a platform model shows privacy-protecting shoppers can be bundled into fuzzy segments and charged a premium for anonymity ("Opting out of data sharing may cost you," W4410534098); motor insurers find that discounts effectively buy back privacy objections, and that explaining the surveillance helps rather than hurts ("Explaining how the tracker works," W7214964045); and freemium AI pricing turns users' own usage into the thing that raises the premium price ("When AI learns from users, the free tier can start eating the business," W7213561739). Taken together: the price you are offered increasingly depends on what a model infers about you and what you refused to tell it.

**Why pitch this now:** Regulators on both sides of the Atlantic have opened inquiries into surveillance and personalized pricing just as research teams start replacing consumer panels with LLM respondents — so the inputs and the outputs of price-setting are both becoming machine-mediated in the same twelve months.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the quiet transfer of price-setting authority from market research to models — what the evidence says goes wrong, why opting out of data sharing can cost money rather than save it, and what a pricing team owes customers when a machine supplies the demand curve. Fits business and marketing decision-makers, with a consumer-facing version for readers who assume privacy settings protect their wallet.

**Potential headlines:**
- What goes wrong when a model, not a shopper, sets the price
- Refusing to share your data can make you the expensive customer
- Nobody asked you what you'd pay, and the price went up anyway

**Potential outlets:**
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — exactly its register for a governance argument about validating AI-generated demand estimates before they reach a price committee.
- **Digiday** — covers the data-deprecation economy and would take the finding that anonymity becomes a segmentation signal platforms can price against.
- **Wired** — runs the surveillance-pricing beat and would use the telematics and fuzzy-segmentation evidence as the spine of a consumer-tech piece.
- **Consumer Reports** — its advocacy reporting on personalized pricing fits the "privacy settings don't protect your wallet" strand directly.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Showing shoppers the math: making hidden tier discounts visible lifted subscriptions on a health platform (Work ID W7220990040):** Demand moved without a single price changing, because customers won't do cross-tier arithmetic themselves — and only for recurring, predictable needs, for a pricing-strategy column aimed at subscription and e-commerce leaders.
- **Grocery subscriptions: shoppers want the mental break more than the time savings (Work ID W7221025098):** "Convenience" is the wrong pitch; the selling point is not having to remember, while lock-in and wrong-quantity fears remain unaddressed, for a retail trade explainer or a grocery e-commerce news brief.
- **The psychology of the subscription you never use but can't cancel (Work ID W7215055600):** Canceling feels like dropping a relationship, not ending a transaction — which is why unused subscriptions survive, for a consumer-psychology explainer in a general-interest outlet, with a churn-strategy sidebar for marketers.
- **When every product looks the same, promotion and CRM are what investors pay for (Work ID W7215085152):** A valuation argument for defending brand and CRM budgets in commoditizing categories — except when the balance sheet is weak, for a CMO/CFO-audience business column.
- **"Leave a 5-star review and get a discount" damages trust more than simply paying for honest feedback (Work ID W7221330457):** One line of copy decides whether a review incentive reads as a thank-you or a bribe, and the most trusting customers punish it hardest, for a marketing-trade news brief or an e-commerce/reputation explainer.
- **Consistent prices across channels build lock-in; consistent promotions do nothing (Work ID W7221526089):** Shoppers forgive app-only deals but not mismatched shelf and online prices — a reason to split price parity from promotional parity in omnichannel roadmaps, for a retail trade explainer.
- **Half of smokers don't flinch at price hikes — but plain packs reach them (Work ID W7215078694):** A market that splits cleanly into a price-responsive minority and a design-responsive majority, with a measurable push toward illicit supply when price is squeezed, for a health-policy piece or a pricing-strategy column on elasticity segmentation.
- **Explaining how the tracker works makes drivers more likely to accept it, not less (Work ID W7214964045):** Transparency about data collection worked as an acquisition tool, and discounts measurably offset privacy objections — the closest thing yet to a price tag on driving data, for a financial-services trade piece or a consumer money column on usage-based insurance.
- **Nearly 4 in 10 cigarettes smoked in Bolivia's big cities are illicit — but taxes aren't the reason (Work ID W7215090900):** Identical national tax rates, wildly different illicit share by city — independent pack-level evidence against the industry's standard anti-tax argument, for a global-health or investigative policy feature.
- **Europe's supermarkets are selling nearly identical plant-based lineups — and pricing them inconsistently (Work ID W7219001667):** Retailers, not manufacturers, are the gatekeepers of the plant-based category, and they're merchandising it as an undifferentiated block with no pricing logic, for a food-industry trade explainer or a category-management piece.
- **Making it cheaper isn't enough: how constant tradeoffs trap low-income shoppers (Work ID W7204257214):** A challenge to bottom-of-the-pyramid orthodoxy — value-tier strategies may erode the social networks that actually keep households solvent, for a general-interest feature on the cost of being poor or a responsible-business column.
- **AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do — and the gap wrecks price optimization (Work ID W7214644774):** Synthetic panels produced plausible numbers and the wrong price, with error direction unpredictable from the product — essential reading for anyone piloting LLM research, for a marketing-analytics trade piece or an insights-industry news feature.
- **For luxury NFTs, logos get clicks but only visual craft earns a price premium (Work ID W7213234135):** Brand prominence drives trial, execution quality drives price — a clean split between the two jobs a digital collectible does, for a luxury or fashion-business trade piece.
- **Opting out of data sharing may cost you: a model says privacy-protecting shoppers can end up paying more (Work ID W4410534098):** Privacy rules may hand platforms a new segmentation lever that prices anonymity at a premium — flag clearly that this is theory, not observed transactions, for a tech-policy or consumer-advocacy explainer.
- **When AI learns from users, the free tier can start eating the business (Work ID W7213561739):** The freemium bargain reverses once adaptive learning works too well, and better AI lets firms raise premium prices rather than share the gains — for a tech-business column on AI pricing models.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Pricing & Promotions — 2026-10-13
**Checked:** 2026-10-13 | **Studies reviewed:** 15
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: Showing shoppers the math: making hidden tier discounts visible lifted subscriptions on a health platform
**Work ID:** W7220990040 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 2: Grocery subscriptions: shoppers want the mental break more than the time savings
**Work ID:** W7221025098 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Drivers and barriers were estimated in separate models** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "researchers tested a value-versus-risk framework for automatic grocery replenishment subscriptions, pitting four benefits (time efficiency, supply reliability, cognitive relief, cost efficiency) against four matching worries (time concerns, supply mismatch, lock-in, financial concerns)"
- **Abstract says:** "Two structural models, a ‘drivers model’ and a ‘barriers model’, were estimated using quota-representative surveys in Germany (N = 493) and the UK (N = 339), complemented by multigroup analysis."
- **Problem:** "Pitting ... against" implies drivers and barriers were pitted head-to-head in one model; the abstract describes two separate structural models whose variance explained is compared.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the team estimated separate 'drivers' and 'barriers' models and compared how much variance each explained."

### Study 3: The psychology of the subscription you never use but can't cancel
**Work ID:** W7215055600 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: When every product looks the same, promotion and CRM are what investors pay for
**Work ID:** W7215085152 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Attenuation described as disappearance** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The advantage disappeared for firms under heavy financial distress, where investors appear to discount the future payoff of relationship and communication investments."
- **Abstract says:** "the stronger value-enhancing effect of intangible differentiation in high-similarity industries is attenuated when firms face high financial distress"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports the effect is weakened (attenuated), not eliminated; 'disappeared' implies a null result that the abstract does not state.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'The advantage was weakened for firms under heavy financial distress'."

### Study 5: "Leave a 5-star review and get a discount" damages trust more than simply paying for honest feedback
**Work ID:** W7221330457 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Unsupported trend claim in consumer angle** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Shoppers increasingly read the incentive behind the review, not just the review."
- **Abstract says:** "These findings demonstrate that consumers respond not only to the presence of review incentives but also to how they are structured and communicated."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a single between-subjects experiment with no time-series or trend data, so 'increasingly' is not supported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop 'increasingly' — e.g. 'In this experiment, people reacted to how the incentive was framed, not just to its presence.'"

### Study 6: Consistent prices across channels build lock-in; consistent promotions do nothing
**Work ID:** W7221526089 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Null result read as consumer preference** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Most shoppers seem relaxed about app-only coupons and store-only specials, but notice when the shelf price and the online price don't match. The former reads as a deal; the latter reads as a trick."
- **Abstract says:** "promotion consistency is related to neither [synergy realisation nor lock-in]"
- **Problem:** A non-significant association between promotion consistency and the two outcomes is not evidence that shoppers are 'relaxed' about inconsistent promotions or that they read them as a deal; this is interpretation beyond the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "State that promotion consistency showed no measurable link to synergy or lock-in in this sample, without inferring how shoppers feel about channel-specific deals."

### Study 7: Half of smokers don't flinch at price hikes — but plain packs reach them
**Work ID:** W7215078694 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline understates the non-price-sensitive share** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Half of smokers don't flinch at price hikes — but plain packs reach them"
- **Abstract says:** "Class II (60%) was not significantly price-sensitive, preferred branded packaging and branded sticks"
- **Problem:** The non-price-sensitive class is 60% of smokers, not half; the headline also implies plain packs 'reach' that group, whereas it was Class I (40%) that preferred plain packaging while Class II preferred branded packs.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rewrite as e.g. '60% of smokers in this study weren't price-sensitive — and the 40% who were preferred plain packs'."

**Issue B. Headline reverses who responds to plain packs** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "but plain packs reach them"
- **Abstract says:** "Class I (40% membership) was price-sensitive ... and preferred plain over branded packaging and sticks with health warnings over branded sticks. Class II (60%) was not significantly price-sensitive, preferred branded packaging and branded sticks"
- **Problem:** The abstract shows the price-insensitive majority preferred branded packaging; it does not show plain packs 'reach' that group. The combined-policy simulation reduces uptake overall, not specifically within Class II.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the two classes respond to opposite levers and that combining price and packaging policies reduced predicted uptake overall by 7.7 points."

### Study 8: Explaining how the tracker works makes drivers more likely to accept it, not less
**Work ID:** W7214964045 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Equal group split not stated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Half received a clear explanation of how telematics technology gathers and uses driving data before evaluating hypothetical policies; half did not."
- **Abstract says:** "1,301 European motor insurance policyholders were randomly assigned either to a control group or to a treatment group that received information explaining the functioning of telematics technology"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state that the allocation was 50/50; the exact split is unverifiable from the abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say participants were randomly assigned to a treatment group that received the explanation or to a control group that did not."

### Study 9: Nearly 4 in 10 cigarettes smoked in Bolivia's big cities are illicit — but taxes aren't the reason
**Work ID:** W7215090900 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mischaracterises the prior 2002 estimate** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "this is the first independent, pack-level estimate for Bolivia since 2002"
- **Abstract says:** "The most recent estimate of illicit trade in Bolivia dates to 2002 and relied on industry-reported sales data. We provide the first independent, direct estimate of illicit cigarette penetration in the country."
- **Problem:** 'First independent ... since 2002' implies the 2002 estimate was also independent; the abstract says it relied on industry-reported sales data and that this is the first independent estimate full stop.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write 'the first independent, pack-level estimate for Bolivia — the only prior figure, from 2002, came from industry-reported sales data'."

### Study 10: Europe's supermarkets are selling nearly identical plant-based lineups — and pricing them inconsistently
**Work ID:** W7219001667 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. 'Almost no fish analogues' overstates 'underrepresented'** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The authors flag thin brand variety, almost no fish analogues, limited recipe and flavor diversity, and inconsistent pricing and category labeling across retailers."
- **Abstract says:** "investing in underrepresented segments such as fish analogues, and increasing recipe-level variety in terms of flavour profiles, culinary traditions and plant protein sources"
- **Problem:** The abstract calls fish analogues an underrepresented segment; it does not report that they are almost absent, and gives no share figure.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'underrepresented fish analogues'."

### Study 11: Making it cheaper isn't enough: how constant tradeoffs trap low-income shoppers
**Work ID:** W7204257214 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Two concepts merged into one** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "which the authors theorize as "consumption entrapment": a self-reinforcing cycle in which repeated inadequate purchases erode the reciprocity, trust and mutual support networks people depend on"
- **Abstract says:** "The study develops the concepts of consumption entrapment and collapsing social capital, demonstrating how repeated consumption inadequacies weaken reciprocity, trust and relational support"
- **Problem:** The abstract presents two separate theoretical contributions — consumption entrapment (a cumulative, self-reinforcing condition) and collapsing social capital. The digest folds the erosion of trust and reciprocity into the definition of entrapment.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword as "which the authors theorize as 'consumption entrapment' alongside a parallel concept of 'collapsing social capital' — repeated inadequate purchases weaken the reciprocity, trust and relational support people depend on.""

### Study 12: AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do — and the gap wrecks price optimization
**Work ID:** W7214644774 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline overstates direction of error** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do — and the gap wrecks price optimization"
- **Abstract says:** "For two more hedonic products, synthetic respondents overstate WTP ... For two more utilitarian products, results are more heterogeneous, ranging from near mean-level correspondence to substantial WTP underestimation."
- **Problem:** Overstatement was found for only two of four products; for the other two the synthetic estimates were accurate or too low. The headline implies a uniform upward bias, which the digest body itself contradicts.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe, e.g. "AI respondents miss real willingness to pay — sometimes high, sometimes low — and the gap undermines price optimization.""

**Issue B. Added emphasis not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the synthetic respondents systematically overstated willingness to pay"
- **Abstract says:** "synthetic respondents overstate WTP and imply overly optimistic demand and profit outcomes"
- **Problem:** "Systematically" adds a claim of consistency the abstract does not make.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "systematically" and simply say the synthetic respondents overstated willingness to pay."

### Study 13: For luxury NFTs, logos get clicks but only visual craft earns a price premium
**Work ID:** W7213234135 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Behavioral language for a stated intention** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "logos get clicks but only visual craft earns a price premium"
- **Abstract says:** "all three visual features significantly increase willingness to buy, whereas only visual quality significantly impacts willingness to pay a price premium"
- **Problem:** "Clicks" suggests observed online behavior; the study measured self-reported willingness to buy in an experiment.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "logos lift buying intent" rather than "logos get clicks.""

**Issue B. Three-way interaction omitted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Brand prominence also moderated typicality: the preference for category-typical NFTs faded when branding was subtle."
- **Abstract says:** "This interaction is further moderated by visual quality, suggesting a joint effect among the visual features."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports that the brand prominence x typicality interaction is itself conditioned by visual quality; the digest stops at the two-way interaction.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add a clause noting the interaction was further moderated by visual quality, indicating the three design cues work jointly."

### Study 14: Opting out of data sharing may cost you: a model says privacy-protecting shoppers can end up paying more
**Work ID:** W4410534098 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Consumer advice not supported by the model** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Comparison shopping across sellers, not just privacy settings, is what protects your wallet."
- **Abstract says:** "data-sharing consumers who prefer third-party sellers may also experience negative spillovers, paying higher prices due to their inclusion in mixed segments ... they may inadvertently lead to higher prices for both anonymous and certain data-sharing consumers, reducing overall consumer welfare"
- **Problem:** The model shows consumers who favor third-party sellers can also be priced up, so it does not establish that shopping across sellers protects buyers. This is prescriptive advice the analysis does not test.
- **Suggested fix:** "Replace with a statement that the model finds no simple consumer defense — even shoppers who prefer third-party sellers can be swept into higher-priced segments."

**Issue B. Consumer welfare conclusion omitted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "tighter data rules may hand platforms a new segmentation lever that raises prices for the very consumers the rules were meant to protect"
- **Abstract says:** "they may inadvertently lead to higher prices for both anonymous and certain data-sharing consumers, reducing overall consumer welfare"
- **Problem:** The abstract's headline implication — a reduction in overall consumer welfare — is not stated; the digest limits the harm to anonymous users.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that the model implies reduced overall consumer welfare, affecting both anonymous and some data-sharing consumers."

### Study 15: When AI learns from users, the free tier can start eating the business
**Work ID:** W7213561739 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Capability-gap finding restated vaguely** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the model implies there's a capability gap you have to actively manage between free and paid"
- **Abstract says:** "Narrowing the base capability gap between versions can also increase profitability by strengthening adaptive learning despite the increased cannibalization."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives a specific directional result — narrowing the gap can raise profits — while the digest's wording is directionless and could be read as advising a wider gap, the opposite of the stated finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "State the result directly: narrowing the capability gap between free and paid can raise profits because it strengthens adaptive learning, even though it increases cannibalization."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Showing shoppers the math: making hidden tier discounts visible lifted subscriptions on a health platform | ✅ Accurate | Design, mechanism checks, moderator and caveats all match the abstract; causal language is appropriately hedged as quasi-experimental. |
| 2 | Grocery subscriptions: shoppers want the mental break more than the time savings | ⚠️ Minor issues | Samples, drivers/barriers and the cognitive-relief finding are reported correctly; only the modelling description is loose. |
| 3 | The psychology of the subscription you never use but can't cancel | ✅ Accurate | Five studies (one survey, four experiments), the retention-specific effect and the acquisition/one-time-purchase boundary conditions are all faithfully reported; caveats correctly flag unreported sample details. |
| 4 | When every product looks the same, promotion and CRM are what investors pay for | ⚠️ Minor issues | Accurate on the core asymmetry and the distress boundary condition, but 'disappeared' overstates 'attenuated'. |
| 5 | "Leave a 5-star review and get a discount" damages trust more than simply paying for honest feedback | ⚠️ Minor issues | Study description, mediation and the disposition-to-trust moderation are accurate, and the marginal direct-effect moderation is flagged; one consumer-angle claim goes beyond the data. |
| 6 | Consistent prices across channels build lock-in; consistent promotions do nothing | ⚠️ Minor issues | Path results and moderation are reported correctly, but the consumer angle reads a null path as positive shopper tolerance. |
| 7 | Half of smokers don't flinch at price hikes — but plain packs reach them | ⚠️ Minor issues | Latent-class percentages, the 7.7pp and 4.2pp figures and sample composition are correct; the headline rounds 60% down to 'half'. |
| 8 | Explaining how the tracker works makes drivers more likely to accept it, not less | ⚠️ Minor issues | Sample, design, direction of effect and the 'modest driver' framing all match; one unverifiable detail about group sizes. |
| 9 | Nearly 4 in 10 cigarettes smoked in Bolivia's big cities are illicit — but taxes aren't the reason | ⚠️ Minor issues | All headline numbers (38.1%, 85%, 54.4%, 10.4%), sample and method match; one phrasing about the 2002 benchmark is slightly off. |
| 10 | Europe's supermarkets are selling nearly identical plant-based lineups — and pricing them inconsistently | ⚠️ Minor issues | Audit scope (748 products, 17 retailers, 5 countries) and the three commercialization clusters are accurate; one descriptor is stronger than the abstract. |
| 11 | Making it cheaper isn't enough: how constant tradeoffs trap low-income shoppers | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, themes and practical implications match the abstract; minor conflation of the paper's two distinct concepts (consumption entrapment vs. collapsing social capital). |
| 12 | AI shoppers say they'll pay more than real shoppers do — and the gap wrecks price optimization | ⚠️ Minor issues | Body text faithfully reports the mixed direction of error, but the headline asserts only over-statement, which holds for the two hedonic products and not the utilitarian ones. |
| 13 | For luxury NFTs, logos get clicks but only visual craft earns a price premium | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, N and main effects are accurate; the headline implies observed clicking behavior and the three-way interaction with visual quality is dropped. |
| 14 | Opting out of data sharing may cost you: a model says privacy-protecting shoppers can end up paying more | ⚠️ Minor issues | Model, mechanism and equilibrium results are reported accurately and the theoretical status is clearly caveated; the consumer-facing advice goes slightly beyond the model. |
| 15 | When AI learns from users, the free tier can start eating the business | ⚠️ Minor issues | Core model results are reported accurately; the marketer angle paraphrases the capability-gap finding loosely and in a direction the abstract does not state. |

**Total issues:** 17 (16 Minor, 1 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 13
**Entries cleared:** 2
